course_title: Practical Exercise on European and Global Legal History
title: Questions and sources, exercise classes I and II

slides.title: What is law?
slides.text: The first question of the exercise class, and also the one it is easiest to slip on, because it looks trivial. THE ANSWER IS NOT ONE DEFINITION BUT A DEMONSTRATION THAT EVERY DEFINITION SELECTS SOMETHING AND PASSES OVER SOMETHING ELSE. Law can be defined as a BODY OF BINDING NORMS GOVERNING CONDUCT IN SOCIETY, WHOSE OBSERVANCE IS ENFORCEABLE. But every element of that sentence is contestable: NORMATIVITY (law says what OUGHT to be, not what is), BINDINGNESS (why does it bind?), ENFORCEABILITY (who enforces it, and what then of international law, where a central coercive power is missing?) and its SOCIAL CHARACTER (ubi societas, ibi ius — where there is society, there is law). IN LEGAL HISTORY THE QUESTION IS PRACTICAL, NOT PHILOSOPHICAL: HOW BROADLY YOU DEFINE LAW DETERMINES WHAT COUNTS AS THE OBJECT OF STUDY. A narrow definition (law = the statutes of a state) excludes customary law, religious law and the law of tribal societies, and thereby turns global legal history into the history of the European state. That is precisely why this course works with a broad conception.

terms.def: Where there is society, there is law — every human community creates norms for itself.

cards.q: What is law — and why is the question practical in global legal history?
cards.a: A body of BINDING NORMS governing conduct in society whose observance is ENFORCEABLE — but every element is contestable (normativity, bindingness, enforceability, social character). IT IS PRACTICAL BECAUSE THE BREADTH OF THE DEFINITION DETERMINES THE OBJECT OF STUDY: a narrow definition (law = state statutes) excludes customary, religious and tribal law, and thereby turns global history into the history of the European state.
cards.topic: Introduction: Methods, Sources, Aims of Legal History

slides.title: What legal history is, and three reasons why it is useful
slides.text: LEGAL HISTORY STUDIES THE LAW OF THE PAST: how it arose, changed and disappeared, and in what relation it stood to the society that carried it. It stands on the border of two disciplines, and that is its tension — the HISTORICAL INTEREST wants to know how things were, the LEGAL INTEREST wants to know what follows from that for today. THREE REASONS WHY IT IS USEFUL TO A LAWYER (exactly as many as the question asks for): (1) UNDERSTANDING THE LAW IN FORCE — today's institutions are historical products and without their origins they are unintelligible (why ownership has the shape it has, where freedom of contract comes from, why private and public law are divided); (2) CRITICAL DISTANCE — what seems natural and necessary turns out to be conditioned by its time and therefore changeable, and that is the strongest remedy against taking the law in force as a given; (3) COMPARATIVE CAPACITY — whoever knows several legal orders in time more easily grasps foreign legal orders in space, which is directly usable in international practice. To these a fourth is often added: legal history TEACHES ONE TO WORK WITH A SOURCE, the very skill the exam tests.

cards.q: What is legal history and what tension is there in it?
cards.a: It studies THE LAW OF THE PAST — how it arose, changed and disappeared, and what relation it had to society. The tension is between the HISTORICAL INTEREST (how things were) and the LEGAL INTEREST (what follows from that for today).
cards.topic: Introduction: Methods, Sources, Aims of Legal History

cards.q: Give three reasons why legal history is useful to a lawyer.
cards.a: 1) UNDERSTANDING THE LAW IN FORCE — today's institutions are historical products and without their origins unintelligible. 2) CRITICAL DISTANCE — what seems natural and necessary turns out to be conditioned by its time, and therefore changeable. 3) COMPARATIVE CAPACITY — whoever knows several orders in time more easily grasps foreign orders in space.

slides.title: Kinds of historical source — with an example of each
slides.text: The question expressly asks for AN EXAMPLE OF EACH KIND, so the bare list is not enough. (1) WRITTEN SOURCES: normative texts (the Code of Hammurabi, the Corpus iuris civilis, the ABGB), charters and treaties (the Golden Bull of Sicily, the Peace of Westphalia), court files and records, juristic literature (glosses, commentaries), but also indirect texts such as chronicles and letters. (2) VISUAL SOURCES: the depiction of a court in the Sachsenspiegel, the allegory of Justice with scales and sword, engravings of executions, portraits of rulers with the imperial regalia. (3) ARTEFACTS (material sources): the pillory, the gallows, the judge's seat, seals and seal-matrices, coins bearing the ruler's title, standard measures on town hall walls. (4) ORAL TRADITION: the recited customary law of societies without writing, judicial formulae handed down orally, witness testimony recorded only later. THE ESSENTIAL DISTINCTION: sources that are LEGAL (created as law) and sources ABOUT LAW (created for another purpose but telling us about law) — a chronicle is not a legal source, but it often says more about how law worked than a code does.

cards.q: Which kinds of historical source does legal history use? An example of each.
cards.a: WRITTEN (the Code of Hammurabi, the Corpus iuris civilis, peace treaties, court files, glosses). VISUAL (the depiction of a court in the Sachsenspiegel, the allegory of Justice, engravings of executions). ARTEFACTS (the pillory, the gallows, seals, coins bearing the ruler's title, standard measures). ORAL TRADITION (recited customary law, judicial formulae, witness testimony).
cards.topic: Introduction: Methods, Sources, Aims of Legal History

cards.q: What is the difference between a legal source and a source about law?
cards.a: A LEGAL SOURCE was created as law (a code, a treaty, a judgment). A SOURCE ABOUT LAW was created for another purpose but tells us about law (a chronicle, a letter, a picture) — and about how law ACTUALLY WORKED it often says more than a code does.
cards.topic: Introduction: Methods, Sources, Aims of Legal History

slides.title: Where the ambition of global legal history runs up against the sources
slides.text: This is a question where the examiner wants EXPRESSLY EXAMPLES OF THE PROBLEMS AND, IF POSSIBLE, SOLUTIONS TOO. Four obstacles. (1) LINGUISTIC: global legal history would require reading sources in Arabic, Chinese, Sanskrit, Hebrew, Latin and dozens of other languages — NO INDIVIDUAL CAN MANAGE THAT, and working with translations means working with a secondary source and with the translator's choices. The solution: INTERNATIONAL COOPERATION AND COLLECTIVE PROJECTS, in which each contributes his own linguistic area. (2) UNEVEN SURVIVAL: European archives are incomparably richer than the sources for pre-colonial Africa or Oceania, which TEMPTS ONE TO CONCLUDE THAT THERE WAS NO LAW THERE — whereas it was merely not written. The solution: to draw in ORAL TRADITION, ARCHAEOLOGY AND ANTHROPOLOGY and to read colonial sources against the grain. (3) CONCEPTUAL: our categories are European. To ask whether China had 'constitutional law' or whether Islamic law knows 'private law' is to MEASURE A FOREIGN ORDER BY A EUROPEAN YARDSTICK and necessarily to conclude that something is 'missing' from it. The solution: FUNCTIONAL COMPARISON — not 'does this order have institution X?' but 'how does this order solve the problem that institution X solves for us?'. (4) THE EUROCENTRISM OF PERIODIZATION: 'antiquity – the Middle Ages – the modern period' is a European scheme that makes no sense elsewhere. The solution: TO WORK WITH LOCAL PERIODIZATIONS and to use the European one consciously as one among many.

cards.q: Which four obstacles stand in the way of global legal history, and what are the solutions?
cards.a: 1) LINGUISTIC — nobody knows all the languages of the sources; the solution is INTERNATIONAL COOPERATION. 2) UNEVEN SURVIVAL — poorer sources tempt one to conclude there was no law there; the solution is ORAL TRADITION, ARCHAEOLOGY, ANTHROPOLOGY. 3) CONCEPTUAL — European categories measure a foreign order by a European yardstick; the solution is FUNCTIONAL COMPARISON. 4) THE EUROCENTRISM OF PERIODIZATION; the solution is local periodizations.
cards.topic: Introduction: Methods, Sources, Aims of Legal History

cards.q: What is functional comparison and why is it used in global legal history?
cards.a: It asks not 'DOES THIS ORDER HAVE INSTITUTION X?' but 'HOW DOES THIS ORDER SOLVE THE PROBLEM THAT INSTITUTION X SOLVES FOR US?'. It is used because European concepts (constitutional law, private law) are conditioned by time and place, and applied directly to a foreign order they necessarily make something appear to be 'missing'.
cards.topic: Introduction: Methods, Sources, Aims of Legal History

slides.title: Method: the interpretation of a written source
slides.text: The principal method of legal history for a written source is the HISTORICAL-CRITICAL METHOD, that is, INTERPRETATION supplemented by SOURCE CRITICISM. Source criticism has two steps: EXTERNAL CRITICISM asks WHETHER THE SOURCE IS GENUINE, who produced it, when, where, and in what form it has survived (original, copy, forgery — the Middle Ages are full of forgeries, and they are not always frauds; often they merely record afterwards what was believed to have long been in force). INTERNAL CRITICISM asks WHAT THE SOURCE SAYS AND WHY IT SAYS IT THIS WAY: what the author's purpose was, for whom the text was intended, what it passes over in silence. Only then comes the INTERPRETATION proper, which is done by the same methods a lawyer knows from the law in force: LINGUISTIC (what the words meant THEN, not today), SYSTEMATIC (where the text stands within the order as a whole), HISTORICAL (what the intention was) and TELEOLOGICAL (what purpose the text was to serve). FURTHER METHODS THE QUESTION ASKS FOR IN ADDITION: the COMPARATIVE METHOD (the same problem in different orders), the STATISTICAL AND QUANTITATIVE (how many judgments, what punishments, how often), PROSOPOGRAPHY (the collective biography of a group — who the judges were, where they came from, what they studied), ORAL HISTORY for recent history, ARCHAEOLOGY AND ICONOGRAPHY for material and pictorial sources.

terms.def: External: is the source genuine, who, when, where. Internal: what it says, why it says it this way, what it passes over.

cards.q: By what method does one work with a written source, and what does it consist of?
cards.a: THE HISTORICAL-CRITICAL: first SOURCE CRITICISM — EXTERNAL (is it genuine? who, when, where, original or forgery) and INTERNAL (what it says, why this way, what it passes over) — and only then INTERPRETATION by the methods a lawyer knows: linguistic (what the words meant THEN), systematic, historical and teleological.
cards.topic: Introduction: Methods, Sources, Aims of Legal History

cards.q: Which further methods besides the interpretation of a source do legal historians use?
cards.a: The COMPARATIVE (the same problem in different orders), the STATISTICAL AND QUANTITATIVE (how many judgments, what punishments), PROSOPOGRAPHY (the collective biography of a group — who the judges were, where from, what they studied), ORAL HISTORY for recent history, ARCHAEOLOGY AND ICONOGRAPHY for material and pictorial sources.
cards.topic: Introduction: Methods, Sources, Aims of Legal History

slides.title: The classical periodization and what is problematic about it
slides.text: THE CLASSICAL PERIODIZATION divides history into ANTIQUITY, THE MIDDLE AGES AND THE MODERN PERIOD, with the usual landmarks of 476 (the fall of the Western Roman Empire), 1492 (the discovery of America) or 1517 (the Reformation), and sometimes 1789 (the French Revolution) as the beginning of modernity. It arose in the RENAISSANCE AND HUMANISM, where the 'MIDDLE AGE' was a CONTEMPTUOUS NAME for the period between antiquity and its rebirth — that is, for something worthless in between. And precisely from that the problems follow. (1) IT IS EVALUATIVE, NOT DESCRIPTIVE: the very word 'Middle Ages' contains the judgment that it is an interval. (2) IT IS EUROCENTRIC: the year 476 means nothing for China, India or the Islamic world; transferred to them it makes no sense. (3) IT FEIGNS SHARP BREAKS where there was continuity — Roman law did not perish in 476 and the Middle Ages did not begin overnight. (4) IT TEMPTS ONE INTO TELEOLOGY, that is, the impression that history was heading somewhere and culminated with us. (5) AND IN LEGAL HISTORY IT DOES NOT FIT THE SUBJECT MATTER: for law the landmarks are different from those of political history — the reception of Roman law from the 12th century, the codifications of the late 18th and early 19th centuries, the constitutional movements of the 19th. That is why legal history is often periodized BY ITS OWN BREAKS, not by political ones.

cards.q: Where does the classical periodization come from and what in its name betrays a judgment?
cards.a: From the RENAISSANCE AND HUMANISM, where the 'MIDDLE AGE' was a CONTEMPTUOUS NAME for the period between antiquity and its rebirth — that is, for a worthless interval. The very word contains a judgment; it is not a description.
cards.topic: Introduction: Methods, Sources, Aims of Legal History

cards.q: What is problematic about the classical periodization? Five points.
cards.a: 1) It is EVALUATIVE, not descriptive. 2) It is EUROCENTRIC — the year 476 means nothing for China, India or the Islamic world. 3) It FEIGNS SHARP BREAKS where there was continuity. 4) It TEMPTS ONE INTO TELEOLOGY, as if history culminated with us. 5) IN LEGAL HISTORY IT DOES NOT FIT THE SUBJECT MATTER — for law the landmarks are different (the reception from the 12th c., the codifications, the constitutional movements).
cards.topic: Introduction: Methods, Sources, Aims of Legal History

slides.title: 'Austria', 'emperor' and the third Rome
slides.text: Three terms with which the examiner shows that WORDS HAVE DIFFERENT CONTENT AT DIFFERENT TIMES. 'AUSTRIA' is not one thing: first a MARCH (Ostarrîchi, first attested in 996) on the eastern edge of the empire, then a DUCHY (the Privilegium minus 1156), then a COLLECTION OF LANDS UNITED IN THE PERSON OF THE RULER — and that is the key, because the Habsburgs did not rule 'Austria' as a state but EACH LAND SEPARATELY, holding a different title in each and with a different law applying in each. Only in 1804 does the AUSTRIAN EMPIRE arise as a single state formation, in 1867 AUSTRIA-HUNGARY, in 1918 the REPUBLIC. 'EMPEROR' (imperator) carries a claim to UNIVERSAL RULE inherited from Rome: the medieval Roman emperor is not 'the king of Germany' but the TEMPORAL HEAD OF CHRISTENDOM beside the pope as its spiritual head; the coronation of Charlemagne in 800 is the TRANSLATIO IMPERII, the transfer of the empire. The title therefore tells us about a claim, not about the extent of actual power. AND MOSCOW AS THE 'THIRD ROME': after the fall of Constantinople in 1453 (the second Rome), the princes of Moscow claim the inheritance of the Orthodox empire — the monk Philotheus writes that 'two Romes have fallen, the third stands, and there will be no fourth'. Basil III and then Ivan IV assume the title TSAR (from 'caesar'). THIS SHOWS THAT THE ROMAN CLAIM WAS NOT ONE AND THAT SEVERAL CENTRES OF POWER COMPETED FOR IT.

terms.def: The transfer of the empire — the idea that the Roman empire did not perish but merely passed to a new bearer.

cards.q: What did 'Austria' mean and why does that matter for legal history?
cards.a: First a MARCH (Ostarrîchi, 996), then a DUCHY (the Privilegium minus 1156), then a COLLECTION OF LANDS UNITED IN THE PERSON OF THE RULER — the Habsburgs ruled EACH LAND SEPARATELY, with a different title in each and A DIFFERENT LAW in each. A single state formation arises only in 1804 (the empire), 1867 Austria-Hungary, 1918 the republic.
cards.topic: Introduction: Methods, Sources, Aims of Legal History

cards.q: What does the title 'emperor' mean and why is Moscow the third Rome?
cards.a: EMPEROR (imperator) carries a claim to UNIVERSAL RULE inherited from Rome — the medieval Roman emperor is the TEMPORAL HEAD OF CHRISTENDOM beside the pope; the coronation of Charlemagne in 800 is the TRANSLATIO IMPERII. After the fall of Constantinople in 1453 the princes of Moscow claim the inheritance of the Orthodox empire (Philotheus: 'two Romes have fallen, the third stands, and there will be no fourth') and assume the title TSAR. It shows that SEVERAL CENTRES COMPETED for the Roman claim.
cards.topic: Introduction: Methods, Sources, Aims of Legal History

slides.title: 'Did the Romans invent law?' And what about Greece?
slides.text: The question is deliberately provocative and THE CORRECT ANSWER IS 'NO, BUT…'. NO, because law is two thousand years older than Rome: the CODE OF HAMMURABI is from the 18th century BC, the Sumerian codes (Ur-Nammu) older still, and every society has legal norms. WHAT THE ROMANS ACTUALLY CREATED IS LEGAL SCHOLARSHIP (IURISPRUDENTIA) — THAT IS, AN INDEPENDENT BODY OF EXPERTS WHO EXPOUND LAW SYSTEMATICALLY, CREATE CONCEPTS AND WRITE SPECIALIST LITERATURE ABOUT IT. That is the difference: elsewhere there were norms, in Rome a DISCIPLINE arose. To this they added an elaborate doctrine of private law (ownership, obligations, succession), the distinction of IUS CIVILE / IUS GENTIUM / IUS NATURALE, and finally CODIFICATION — Justinian's Corpus iuris civilis (529–534), through which the whole work survived. AND GREECE? The Greeks DID NOT CREATE LEGAL SCHOLARSHIP and their law remained fragmented among the city states. But there other things have their roots: THE PHILOSOPHY OF LAW AND JUSTICE (Plato, Aristotle and his distinction of DISTRIBUTIVE and COMMUTATIVE justice), THE IDEA OF NATURAL LAW (the Sophists, the Stoics — through whom it passes to the Romans and on into the whole European tradition), DEMOCRACY AND WRITTEN LEGISLATION as an instrument of the city (Draco, Solon) and CONSTITUTIONAL THINKING, that is, the analysis of forms of government.

cards.q: Did the Romans invent law?
cards.a: NO — law is older (Hammurabi 18th c. BC, the Sumerian codes older still). WHAT THEY ACTUALLY CREATED IS LEGAL SCHOLARSHIP (IURISPRUDENTIA): an independent body of experts who expound law systematically, create concepts and write literature about it. Elsewhere there were NORMS, in Rome a DISCIPLINE arose. To this, the doctrine of private law, the distinction ius civile / gentium / naturale and codification (the Corpus iuris civilis, 529–534).
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

cards.q: What has its roots in Greek legal thinking?
cards.a: THE PHILOSOPHY OF LAW AND JUSTICE (Plato, Aristotle with DISTRIBUTIVE and COMMUTATIVE justice), THE IDEA OF NATURAL LAW (the Sophists, the Stoics — through them to the Romans and into the whole European tradition), DEMOCRACY AND WRITTEN LEGISLATION (Draco, Solon) and CONSTITUTIONAL THINKING. Legal scholarship, however, the Greeks DID NOT create, and their law remained fragmented among the city states.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

slides.title: Non-Western legal cultures, and why Mesopotamia
slides.text: THE 'NON-WESTERN' LEGAL CULTURES the course covers: the MESOPOTAMIAN (Sumerian, Babylonian, Assyrian), the EGYPTIAN, the JEWISH, the ISLAMIC, the CHINESE, the INDIAN (Hindu), and further the legal cultures without writing in Africa, the Americas and Oceania. The very label 'non-Western' is, however, problematic, BECAUSE IT DEFINES THE WHOLE REST OF THE WORLD NEGATIVELY IN RELATION TO THE WEST — which is exactly the Eurocentrism the course is meant to avoid. WHY MESOPOTAMIA WAS SUCH FERTILE GROUND FOR THE EMERGENCE OF LEGAL NORMS: (1) IRRIGATION AGRICULTURE between the Euphrates and the Tigris required THE COORDINATION OF LARGE NUMBERS OF PEOPLE in building and maintaining canals and distributing water — and where coordination is required, there must be rules; (2) A HIGH DENSITY OF SETTLEMENT AND CITIES, that is, the coexistence of people who do not know one another and for whom kinship norms do not suffice; (3) LONG-DISTANCE TRADE, which needs enforceable contracts, weights and measures; (4) and above all THE INVENTION OF WRITING (cuneiform, from the end of the 4th millennium BC) — only the written word makes it possible to preserve a norm, to promulgate it and to invoke it. THE LAWS, CODES AND SOURCES THAT CAN BE NAMED: the LAWS OF UR-NAMMU (around 2100 BC, the oldest surviving code), the LAWS OF LIPIT-ISHTAR, the LAWS OF ESHNUNNA, the CODE OF HAMMURABI (around 1750 BC), the MIDDLE ASSYRIAN LAWS, the HITTITE LAWS — plus tens of thousands of clay tablets with contracts, court records and letters.

terms.def: The belt of fertile land from the Persian Gulf through Mesopotamia and the Levant to Egypt — the cradle of agriculture, cities and writing.

cards.q: Why was Mesopotamia such fertile ground for the emergence of legal norms? Four reasons.
cards.a: 1) IRRIGATION AGRICULTURE required THE COORDINATION of many people on canals and the distribution of water. 2) A HIGH DENSITY OF SETTLEMENT AND CITIES — the coexistence of people who do not know one another, where kinship norms do not suffice. 3) LONG-DISTANCE TRADE needing enforceable contracts, weights and measures. 4) THE INVENTION OF WRITING (cuneiform, from the end of the 4th millennium BC) — only the written word preserves a norm, promulgates it and allows it to be invoked.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

cards.q: Name the Mesopotamian law codes.
cards.a: The LAWS OF UR-NAMMU (around 2100 BC, THE OLDEST SURVIVING), the LAWS OF LIPIT-ISHTAR, the LAWS OF ESHNUNNA, the CODE OF HAMMURABI (around 1750 BC), the MIDDLE ASSYRIAN LAWS and the HITTITE LAWS — plus tens of thousands of clay tablets with contracts and court records.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

cards.q: Why is the label 'non-Western legal cultures' problematic?
cards.a: Because it DEFINES THE WHOLE REST OF THE WORLD NEGATIVELY IN RELATION TO THE WEST — it makes the West the standard and everything else a deviation. It is exactly the Eurocentrism that global legal history is meant to avoid.

slides.title: The Code of Hammurabi
slides.text: THE CODE OF HAMMURABI (around 1750 BC) is a collection of legal propositions of the Babylonian king HAMMURABI, carved IN CUNEIFORM ON A BASALT STELE more than two metres high; it is today in the LOUVRE, where it came after French archaeologists found it in 1901 at SUSA — that is, not at Babylon, because the Elamites had carried it off as spoils of war. It consists of a PROLOGUE, some 282 LEGAL PROPOSITIONS AND AN EPILOGUE. In the relief above the text, SHAMASH, the god of the sun and of justice, hands the king the insignia of power — THE LEGITIMATION IS THEREFORE DIVINE, but the text itself is secular. The legal propositions have the CASUISTIC FORM 'IF — THEN' (šumma), do not formulate general principles but resolve individual cases, and cover criminal law, family and property relations, prices and wages, and the liability of craftsmen and physicians alike. The best-known principle is the TALION, 'an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth' — BUT NOTE, THE TALION APPLIES ONLY BETWEEN EQUALS: the punishment depends on the STATUS of the offender and of the victim (awīlum — a free man, muškēnum — a dependant, wardum — a slave), so that for the same injury done to a slave compensation is paid, not retaliation. AND A CONTESTED QUESTION WORTH KNOWING: IT IS NOT CERTAIN WHETHER IT WAS A CODE IN FORCE IN TODAY'S SENSE — in the surviving court records the parties practically never invoke it, so it may rather be a COLLECTION OF MODEL DECISIONS, a ROYAL SELF-PRESENTATION as a just ruler, or both.

terms.def: Retaliation in kind — 'an eye for an eye'; in the Code of Hammurabi it applies only between persons of the same status.

cards.q: What is the Code of Hammurabi and what does it look like?
cards.a: A collection of legal propositions of the Babylonian king Hammurabi (around 1750 BC), carved IN CUNEIFORM ON A BASALT STELE; found in 1901 at SUSA (where the Elamites had carried it off), today in the LOUVRE. A PROLOGUE, some 282 LEGAL PROPOSITIONS, an EPILOGUE. In the relief the god SHAMASH hands the king the insignia of power — the legitimation is DIVINE, the text secular. The propositions are CASUISTIC, 'if — then'.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

cards.q: How exactly does the talion work in Hammurabi and what is contested about the code?
cards.a: THE TALION APPLIES ONLY BETWEEN EQUALS — the punishment depends on STATUS (awīlum a free man, muškēnum a dependant, wardum a slave), so that for injury done to a slave COMPENSATION is paid, not retaliation. WHAT IS CONTESTED is whether it was a code in force at all: in the court records the parties practically never invoke it, so it may be a COLLECTION OF MODEL DECISIONS or a ROYAL SELF-PRESENTATION as a just ruler.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

slides.title: The Fertile Crescent
slides.text: The 'FERTILE CRESCENT' is a term introduced in 1916 by the American orientalist JAMES HENRY BREASTED for the BELT OF FERTILE LAND IN THE SHAPE OF A SICKLE which runs FROM THE PERSIAN GULF UP THE EUPHRATES AND THE TIGRIS THROUGH MESOPOTAMIA, then north-west across present-day SYRIA, curving down through the LEVANT (Lebanon, Israel, Palestine, Jordan) AND ENDING IN EGYPT AT THE NILE; it is bounded to the south by the Arabian desert and to the north by the mountains of Anatolia and Iran. IT MATTERS FOR LEGAL HISTORY BECAUSE IT IS THE REGION WHERE EVERYTHING LAW NEEDS IN ORDER TO ARISE CAME TOGETHER FOR THE FIRST TIME: the Neolithic revolution and settled agriculture, the domestication of animals, the first cities, state organization, long-distance trade and writing. From there come the oldest law codes, and at the same time the three monotheistic religions whose legal orders the course covers.

cards.q: What is the Fertile Crescent and why does it matter in legal history?
cards.a: A sickle-shaped belt of fertile land FROM THE PERSIAN GULF UP THE EUPHRATES AND THE TIGRIS, across Syria and curving through the LEVANT into EGYPT (the term introduced by James Henry Breasted in 1916). It matters because there EVERYTHING LAW NEEDS CAME TOGETHER FOR THE FIRST TIME: settled agriculture, the first cities, state organization, long-distance trade and WRITING — and from there come the oldest codes and the three monotheistic religions.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

slides.title: The diaspora and the sources of Jewish law
slides.text: 'DIASPORA' is Greek for DISPERSION and denotes the life of Jewish communities outside the land of Israel — after the destruction of the FIRST TEMPLE (586 BC, the Babylonian captivity) and definitively after the destruction of the SECOND TEMPLE IN AD 70 and the defeat of the Bar Kokhba revolt (135). THE CONSEQUENCES FOR LAW ARE FUNDAMENTAL AND ARE EXACTLY WHAT THE QUESTION ASKS ABOUT: (1) WITH THE TEMPLE PERISHED THE WHOLE SACRIFICIAL CULT AND WITH IT THE PRIESTHOOD — religion shifted from the temple to the SYNAGOGUE AND TO LEARNING, and the authority became, instead of the priest, the SCHOLAR (the RABBI). (2) WITH THE STATE PERISHED THE POSSIBILITY OF ENFORCING LAW BY THE STATE; Jewish law became a COMMUNAL law, whose bindingness rests on membership of the community and whose harshest sanction is EXCLUSION (HEREM). (3) DISPERSION meant that the communities lived under foreign rulers and legal orders — hence the principle 'DINA DE-MALKHUTA DINA', THE LAW OF THE KINGDOM IS LAW, that is, the recognition of the secular law of the country within its own sphere. (4) And above all: LAW BECAME THE CHIEF BOND OF A DISPERSED PEOPLE — without territory and without a state, identity was held together precisely by the observance of the commandments. THE PRINCIPAL WRITTEN SOURCE is the TORAH, the Five Books of Moses (the Pentateuch), the written Torah. To it belongs the ORAL TORAH, finally written down in the MISHNAH (around AD 200) and, with its commentary (the GEMARA), forming the TALMUD — the Babylonian (the more authoritative) and the Jerusalem. Further sources are the MIDRASH (the exposition of Scripture), the RESPONSA (SHE'ELOT U-TESHUVOT, the rabbis' answers to communities' questions, that is, living practice), and the later CODIFICATIONS: Maimonides' MISHNEH TORAH (12th c.) and Caro's SHULCHAN ARUCH (16th c.).

terms.def: 'The law of the kingdom is law' — the recognition of the secular law of the country within its own sphere.
Exclusion from the community — the harshest sanction of a law without state coercion.

cards.q: What does diaspora mean and what four consequences did it have for Jewish law?
cards.a: Greek for DISPERSION — life outside the land of Israel after the destruction of the first (586 BC) and second Temple (AD 70). 1) THE END OF THE TEMPLE = the end of the sacrificial cult and the priesthood, the authority became the SCHOLAR. 2) THE END OF THE STATE = law cannot be enforced by the state, it becomes COMMUNAL, with HEREM as its harshest sanction. 3) Life under foreign rulers = the principle DINA DE-MALKHUTA DINA. 4) LAW BECAME THE CHIEF BOND OF A DISPERSED PEOPLE.
cards.topic: Jewish Legal History

cards.q: Name the sources of Jewish law.
cards.a: The TORAH (the Five Books of Moses) as the written Torah; the ORAL TORAH written down in the MISHNAH (around AD 200), which with the GEMARA forms the TALMUD (Babylonian and Jerusalem); the MIDRASH (the exposition of Scripture); the RESPONSA (she'elot u-teshuvot — the rabbis' answers to communities' questions); the codifications MISHNEH TORAH (Maimonides, 12th c.) and SHULCHAN ARUCH (Caro, 16th c.).
cards.topic: Jewish Legal History

slides.title: 'Jewish law is governed by people, not by rules'
slides.text: This is a question that has come up in the exam, and the required reading (BEN-MENAHEM) answers it directly. The sentence IS NOT A CRITICISM but a DESCRIPTION OF THE WAY IN WHICH JEWISH LAW DETERMINES WHAT APPLIES. The arguments for it: (1) LAW IS ESSENTIALLY THE INTERPRETATION of a revealed text, and since interpretation is a human act, what decides is THE AUTHORITY OF THE INTERPRETER, not the text itself. (2) THE TALMUD PRESERVES MINORITY OPINIONS TOO, which means that beside the 'valid' rule the one that did not prevail is also recorded — law is therefore not presented as a closed body of rules but as a CONTINUING DISPUTATION. (3) The famous example is THE OVEN OF AKHNAI (Bava Metzia 59b), where Rabbi Eliezer supports his view by miracles and finally by a VOICE FROM HEAVEN — and Rabbi Joshua answers with the words 'LO BA-SHAMAYIM HI', IT IS NOT IN HEAVEN: the Torah was given to human beings, and so its interpretation is decided by THE MAJORITY OF THE SCHOLARS, not by a heavenly voice. It is told that God then smiled and said 'MY CHILDREN HAVE DEFEATED ME'. (4) The institution of the RESPONSA means that law is made by the answers of particular authorities to particular questions, that is, from below and continuously. (5) And the principle that A RABBINICAL COURT MAY IN CERTAIN CIRCUMSTANCES EVEN SET ASIDE A COMMANDMENT, if that is needed to preserve the order. THE COUNTER-ARGUMENT THAT BELONGS IN A COMPLETE ANSWER: precisely because the text is held to be revealed and unchangeable, the bond to it is extraordinarily strong — the interpreter may not create at will and is himself subject to the rules of interpretation. THE CORRECT ANSWER IS THEREFORE: YES, IF BY THAT WE MEAN THAT THE CONTENT OF THE LAW IS DECIDED BY HUMAN INTERPRETIVE AUTHORITY AND NOT BY THE AUTOMATIC APPLICATION OF A TEXT.

terms.def: 'It is not in heaven' — the Torah was given to human beings, so its interpretation is decided by the majority of the scholars, not by a voice from heaven.

cards.q: In what sense is Jewish law 'governed by people, not by rules'?
cards.a: In that THE CONTENT OF THE LAW IS DECIDED BY HUMAN INTERPRETIVE AUTHORITY AND NOT BY THE AUTOMATIC APPLICATION OF A TEXT: law is the interpretation of a revealed text, the Talmud preserves MINORITY OPINIONS too (law as a continuing disputation), the responsa make law from below, and according to THE OVEN OF AKHNAI the MAJORITY OF THE SCHOLARS decides even against a voice from heaven.
cards.topic: Jewish Legal History

cards.q: What is the Oven of Akhnai and what is its point?
cards.a: A Talmudic story (Bava Metzia 59b): Rabbi Eliezer supports his view by miracles and finally by a VOICE FROM HEAVEN, but Rabbi Joshua answers 'LO BA-SHAMAYIM HI' — IT IS NOT IN HEAVEN. The Torah was given to human beings, so its interpretation is decided by THE MAJORITY OF THE SCHOLARS. God, it is said, smiled and said 'MY CHILDREN HAVE DEFEATED ME'.
cards.topic: Jewish Legal History

cards.q: What counter-argument belongs in a complete answer?
cards.a: That precisely because the text is held to be REVEALED AND UNCHANGEABLE, the bond to it is EXTRAORDINARILY STRONG — the interpreter may not create at will and is himself subject to the rules of interpretation. 'Governed by people' therefore does not mean arbitrariness.
cards.topic: Jewish Legal History

slides.title: The rise of early Islamic law and its features
slides.text: WHEN, WHERE AND HOW: Islamic law arises on the ARABIAN PENINSULA in the 7TH CENTURY, beginning with MUHAMMAD'S ACTIVITY IN MECCA (from 610) AND ESPECIALLY IN MEDINA (after the HIJRA IN 622, from which the Islamic era is counted). In Medina Muhammad was not only a prophet but also the LEADER OF THE COMMUNITY AND ITS JUDGE, so that revelation and legal decision-making merge. After his death (632) it spreads with the ARAB CONQUESTS through Syria, Iraq, Persia, Egypt and North Africa as far as Spain, and in doing so takes over much from PRE-ISLAMIC CUSTOM AND FROM THE ADMINISTRATIVE PRACTICES OF THE CONQUERED TERRITORIES (Byzantine and Sasanian). THE FEATURES OF EARLY ISLAMIC LAW: (1) A RELIGIOUS ORIGIN AND CLAIM — law is part of the revealed will of God, not the creation of a legislator, and is therefore in principle UNALTERABLE BY HUMAN BEINGS. (2) SCHOLARLY, NOT STATE — law is developed by the ULEMA (the scholars) in the schools, not by the ruler; the caliph executes the law but does not make it. (3) CASUISTIC AND DISCURSIVE — it arises by resolving cases and recording disagreements (IKHTILAF), so that here too disputation counts for more than a code. (4) IT DOES NOT SEPARATE LAW FROM RELIGION OR FROM ETHICS — a single act is evaluated on a five-point scale from obligatory to forbidden. (5) GRADUAL SYSTEMATIZATION: in the 8th–9th centuries the LEGAL SCHOOLS (MADHAHIB) arise and the doctrine of the sources of law, founded precisely by AL-SHAFI'I.

terms.def: Muhammad's departure from Mecca to Medina in 622; the beginning of the Islamic era.
Disagreement among the scholars — in Islamic law recorded, not eliminated.

cards.q: When, where and how did Islamic law arise?
cards.a: On the ARABIAN PENINSULA in the 7TH CENTURY: through Muhammad's activity in Mecca (from 610) and especially in MEDINA after the HIJRA IN 622, where he was at once prophet, LEADER OF THE COMMUNITY AND JUDGE. After his death (632) it spreads with the Arab conquests and takes over PRE-ISLAMIC CUSTOM AND THE ADMINISTRATIVE PRACTICES of the conquered Byzantine and Sasanian territories.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

cards.q: What are the features of early Islamic law?
cards.a: 1) A RELIGIOUS ORIGIN — law is the revealed will of God, in principle UNALTERABLE by human beings. 2) SCHOLARLY, NOT STATE — developed by the ULEMA in the schools; the caliph executes but does not make law. 3) CASUISTIC AND DISCURSIVE, recording disagreements (IKHTILAF). 4) IT DOES NOT SEPARATE LAW FROM RELIGION OR ETHICS. 5) GRADUAL SYSTEMATIZATION in the 8th–9th centuries: the legal schools and the doctrine of the sources.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

slides.title: Source: al-Shafi'i, the Risala — who he was and which school
slides.text: THE SOURCE: 'Every tradition transmitted by trustworthy persons as going back to the Prophet is authoritative and can be rejected only where another authoritative tradition from the Prophet contradicts it… where both are equally reliable, the one more in accordance with the Qur'an and with the remaining undisputed parts of the Prophet's sunna is to be chosen; traditions from other persons have no weight in the face of a tradition from the Prophet.' (the Risala, 2nd century of the hijra / 8th century AD, quoted from J. Schacht, The Origins of Muhammadan Jurisprudence, 1950, p. 12.) WHO HE WAS: MUHAMMAD IBN IDRIS AL-SHAFI'I (767–820), a jurist active in Iraq, the Hijaz and finally in Egypt, regarded as the FOUNDER OF ISLAMIC LEGAL SCIENCE (USUL AL-FIQH), that is, of the doctrine of the sources of law; his work the RISALA is the first systematic account of where law comes from. THE SCHOOL THAT LOOKS TO HIM IS THE SHAFI'I. THE OTHER SUNNI SCHOOLS: the HANAFI (Abu Hanifa, the most widespread, the law of the Ottoman Empire — and therefore the basis of the MAJALLA), the MALIKI (Malik ibn Anas, North and West Africa), the HANBALI (Ahmad ibn Hanbal, the strictest, the Arabian peninsula). Among the SHIITES the principal school is the JA'FARI. The differences between the schools are not heresy: ALL ARE RECOGNIZED AS VALID, which is precisely that feature of ikhtilaf.

terms.def: The doctrine of the sources of law — the roots of legal science; its founder is al-Shafi'i.

cards.q: Who was al-Shafi'i and why does he matter?
cards.a: MUHAMMAD IBN IDRIS AL-SHAFI'I (767–820), a jurist active in Iraq, the Hijaz and Egypt, regarded as the FOUNDER OF ISLAMIC LEGAL SCIENCE (USUL AL-FIQH) — the doctrine of the sources of law. His RISALA is the first systematic account of where law comes from. The SHAFI'I school looks to him.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

cards.q: Name the Islamic legal schools.
cards.a: SUNNI: the HANAFI (Abu Hanifa, the most widespread, the law of the Ottoman Empire and the basis of the Majalla), the MALIKI (Malik ibn Anas, North and West Africa), the SHAFI'I (al-Shafi'i), the HANBALI (Ahmad ibn Hanbal, the strictest, the Arabian peninsula). Among the SHIITES the JA'FARI. The differences ARE NOT HERESY — all are recognized as valid.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

slides.title: Source: the Qur'an, the sunna and the hierarchy of sources
slides.text: The second part of the question on the Risala. The QUR'AN is for Muslims the LITERAL, UNCREATED WORD OF GOD revealed to Muhammad through the archangel Gabriel and gathered into an authoritative form under the caliph Uthman; it contains 114 suras, but THERE ARE ONLY A FEW HUNDRED LEGAL VERSES, so that by itself it does not constitute a legal order. The SUNNA is the 'CUSTOM' of the Prophet, that is, what Muhammad said, did or tacitly approved; it is transmitted in individual reports called HADITH, each of which has a TEXT (MATN) and a CHAIN OF TRANSMITTERS (ISNAD) — and it is precisely the reliability of the isnad that decides whether a hadith is acceptable. THE FURTHER SOURCES OF SHARIA: IJMA (the consensus of the scholars of the community) and QIYAS (analogy); in some schools further IJTIHAD (independent effort to find a solution), ISTIHSAN (preference for the more equitable solution) and MASLAHA (the common good). WHAT AL-SHAFI'I SAYS ABOUT THEIR RELATION IN THE QUOTED EXTRACT: (1) a tradition going back to THE PROPHET is authoritative and can be rejected only by another tradition from the Prophet; (2) where reliability is equal, the one MORE IN ACCORDANCE WITH THE QUR'AN AND THE UNDISPUTED SUNNA is chosen — the Qur'an thus serves as the standard; (3) traditions from PERSONS OTHER than the Prophet (that is, from the Companions, the Successors, local authorities) HAVE NO WEIGHT IN THE FACE OF A PROPHETIC TRADITION. By this al-Shafi'i SUBORDINATED LOCAL LEGAL CUSTOM TO A SINGLE STANDARD, and that is his chief historical achievement.

terms.def: The chain of transmitters of a hadith and its actual text; acceptability is decided by the reliability of the isnad.

cards.q: What is the Qur'an and what is the sunna?
cards.a: The QUR'AN is the LITERAL, UNCREATED WORD OF GOD revealed to Muhammad and gathered under the caliph Uthman; 114 suras, but ONLY A FEW HUNDRED LEGAL VERSES, so by itself it does not constitute a legal order. The SUNNA is the CUSTOM OF THE PROPHET — what he said, did or tacitly approved; it is transmitted in HADITH, each with a TEXT (MATN) and a CHAIN OF TRANSMITTERS (ISNAD).
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

cards.q: What does al-Shafi'i say about the relation of the sources and what was its historical effect?
cards.a: 1) A tradition going back to THE PROPHET is authoritative and can be rejected only by another prophetic tradition. 2) Where reliability is equal, the one MORE IN ACCORDANCE WITH THE QUR'AN and the undisputed sunna prevails — the Qur'an is the standard. 3) Traditions from PERSONS OTHER than the Prophet have no weight. By this he SUBORDINATED LOCAL LEGAL CUSTOM TO A SINGLE STANDARD.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

cards.q: What are the further sources of sharia besides the Qur'an and the sunna?
cards.a: IJMA (the consensus of the scholars of the community) and QIYAS (analogy); in some schools further IJTIHAD (independent effort to find a solution), ISTIHSAN (preference for the more equitable solution) and MASLAHA (the common good).
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

slides.title: Is sharia only a legal order, or a moral one as well?
slides.text: The last sub-question on the source, and the one that asks for AN ARGUED OPINION OF ONE'S OWN. THE ANSWER IS: BOTH, AND THE DISTINCTION BETWEEN LAW AND MORALITY THAT WE TAKE FOR GRANTED IS HERE UNUSABLE. The reasons: (1) SHARIA LITERALLY MEANS 'THE WAY TO THE WATERING PLACE', that is, the right way through life as a whole, not a body of enforceable norms. (2) IT GOVERNS RITUAL DUTIES (IBADAT — prayer, fasting, pilgrimage, alms) JUST AS MUCH AS RELATIONS BETWEEN PEOPLE (MU'AMALAT — contracts, marriage, succession, punishment), and both are part of one order. (3) The evaluation of conduct has FIVE DEGREES, which show that the scale is broader than 'permitted/forbidden': OBLIGATORY (WAJIB / FARD), RECOMMENDED (MANDUB), INDIFFERENT (MUBAH), REPREHENSIBLE (MAKRUH) AND FORBIDDEN (HARAM) — and neither the recommended nor the reprehensible is legally enforceable, and yet both belong to sharia. (4) The sanction is not merely earthly: the final reckoning is in the WORLD TO COME, which for observance is often a stronger motive than a court. THE COUNTER-ARGUMENT, FOR COMPLETENESS: part of sharia is wholly legal in our sense — it has a court (the QADI), procedure, evidence and enforceable sanctions (the HUDUD), and in practice it was precisely this part that separated off and was codified in the modern states. A DISTINCTION WORTH KNOWING: SHARIA is the ideal divine order; FIQH is the HUMAN UNDERSTANDING of that order, that is, legal science — and what is fallible and multiform is fiqh, not sharia.

terms.def: Sharia is the ideal divine order; fiqh is the human understanding of that order, that is, legal science — fallible and multiform.

cards.q: Is sharia only a legal order or a moral one as well? Give reasons.
cards.a: BOTH — our distinction between law and morality is here unusable. Sharia means 'THE WAY TO THE WATERING PLACE', the right way through life; it governs RITUAL DUTIES (ibadat) just as much as RELATIONS BETWEEN PEOPLE (mu'amalat); it evaluates conduct in FIVE DEGREES, of which the recommended and the reprehensible are NOT ENFORCEABLE; and the final sanction is IN THE WORLD TO COME.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

cards.q: Which five degrees of the evaluation of conduct does sharia know?
cards.a: OBLIGATORY (wajib / fard), RECOMMENDED (mandub), INDIFFERENT (mubah), REPREHENSIBLE (makruh) and FORBIDDEN (haram). Neither the recommended nor the reprehensible is legally enforceable, and yet both belong to sharia.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

cards.q: What is the difference between sharia and fiqh?
cards.a: SHARIA is the IDEAL DIVINE ORDER. FIQH is the HUMAN UNDERSTANDING of that order, that is, legal science. What is FALLIBLE AND MULTIFORM (and on which the schools differ) is FIQH, not sharia.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law
